title: Compliance Rail for Verified Bio-AI Labs
one_liner: A 'SOC 2 for AI-directed biology': fast dossiers plus continuous evidence collection that let small labs qualify for, and keep, verified access to frontier bio-AI.
customer: Small biotechs, CROs, academic cores and AI-bio startups applying to verification programs (Anthropic expects hundreds of organizations in week one); later insurers and pharma partners that request attestations.
problem: Trend chain: frontier providers now gate relaxed bio safeguards behind credential, security and ethics-oversight review. Next, each provider and government runs a slightly different program. Then small labs discover they lack security staff, an oversight committee, or records separating AI proposal, human edit and robot execution (a gap Lab Manager flags, since CDC and WHO frameworks predate autonomous systems). Each application becomes bespoke paperwork.
solution: Week 1: a 5-day 'verification-ready' dossier covering security-control mapping (SOC 2 and ISO 27001-lite), personnel credential packet, data-retention and access configuration, and a dual-use risk register. Optionally add a rent-an-oversight-committee: an independent biosafety and dual-use review board with documented minutes. Month 3 onward: connectors to ELN, LIMS, robot logs and AI-provider logs produce an audit trail and a portable attestation that is reused across providers.
why_now: Anthropic's Life Sciences Verification Program launched Sept 17, 2026, with 30-day data retention and 'hundreds of organizations' expected in the first week. Other providers are likely to follow (an inference). Autonomous labs are multiplying with no accountability standard.
revenue_model: $3-8k per dossier, $1.5-4k/month for oversight-committee and evidence subscription, and per-attestation fees from providers or insurers.
non_obvious_insight: Relaxed safeguards become a competitive credential the way SOC 2 became table stakes in SaaS. The bottleneck is not the AI provider's review but small organizations' inability to package proof. Once two or more providers run programs, a portable attestation beats bespoke applications, and the evidence stream also feeds insurers.
first_30_days: Turn the public criteria into a 40-point readiness checklist. Sell a $1.5k readiness review to 20 startups via SynBioBeta and LinkedIn. Partner with an IBC or biosafety consultancy for the oversight-committee product. Ship the dossier template.

title: Hard-Stop Fuse and Warranty for AI Cloud Bills
one_liner: A free scanner finds unrestricted legacy Google/Firebase and Bedrock exposure, installs a real hard kill-switch, and later sells a capped bill-shock warranty only to accounts that have the fuse installed.
customer: Seed-stage startups, solo developers and small agencies running LLM calls on GCP/Firebase or AWS Bedrock, including anyone running coding agents unattended. They pay $29-49/month per cloud account for the fuse and monitoring, and a small warranty premium later.
problem: Cloud providers ship alerts and credits, not hard caps, and they often refuse refunds. A Bedrock user ran up $37,901.73 through a LiteLLM + prompt-caching miss and asked 'why can I not say this IAM principal may spend at most $200/month'. A 2016 Firebase Android key generated $67k of Gemini charges in 19 hours, and Google support said it was 'unable to make adjustments'. A Claude Code user burned $2,000+ without noticing. A founder's $4,200 fraudulent Gemini charge was followed by suspension of a $1M ARR company's whole Google Cloud project.
solution: Step 1, a read-only CLI/web scanner that lists unrestricted API keys, projects with Gemini or Bedrock enabled, forgotten legacy Firebase keys (which the May 2024 auto-restriction policy missed in at least one documented case), and missing budget actions. Step 2, a one-click installer for hard stops: key restrictions and quota overrides on GCP, and on AWS Budget Actions that attach an IAM/SCP deny on model invocation. Step 3, per-minute anomaly detection that trips the fuse in seconds, not at the next daily billing rollup. Step 4, once an account has run fused for 30+ days, a capped bill-shock warranty (start at $5k, backed by a small reserve, later an MGA or reinsurer) priced from the loss data the fuse collects.
why_now: Unattended agents with huge contexts and Opus-class pricing turned ordinary integration mistakes into five-figure invoices in 2026. Gemini access now hangs off keys created years before Gemini existed. Google and AWS are visibly not shipping hard caps: the April 2026 $67k Gemini case was denied adjustment as of May 2026, and the $37.9k Bedrock case is from April 2026.
revenue_model: Free scan (lead gen). $29/month per cloud account for fuse plus monitoring, $49 for multi-project agencies. $199 one-off audit-and-install for agencies. Warranty add-on priced at roughly 2-4% of the covered limit per year, sold only to fused accounts.
non_obvious_insight: The clouds have shown the market will not get hard caps or reliable refunds from them, so the insurable unit is a fused account, not a customer. The technical control doubles as underwriting, and every victim thread is a warm lead. Evidence: $37,901.73 Bedrock bill with the 'hard spend limit' complaint https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47933355; $67k in 19 hours with Google denying adjustment and other victims reporting $13,000 and £2,700 https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/unexpected-67k-gemini-api-spike-in-19-hours-2016-firebase-provisioned-android-key-not-covered-by-googles-may-2024-auto-restriction-policy/142717; $1M ARR startup suspended after a compromised key https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48396596; $2,000+ Claude Code invoice https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46851021. Caveat: refunds are not reliably obtainable, so do not lead with a claims-desk model.
first_30_days: Week 1-2: build the GCP key/Gemini exposure scanner on top of Cloud Asset Inventory and publish 'Check your 2016 Firebase keys' on HN and the Google AI forum thread. Week 3: add an AWS CloudFormation one-click Budget Action deny for Bedrock. Week 4: DM the authors and repliers of the public bill-shock threads, plus agencies, and offer a $199 audit-and-install to the first 20; convert them to $29/month monitoring. Log every trip event and near-miss to build the actuarial base for the warranty.

title: Visitor-Levy Back Office for Councils
one_liner: White-label registration, returns, audit and enforcement software plus a service desk that lets local councils run a new tourist levy without building it.
customer: Local authorities that have just gained the power to levy visitors: Scottish councils, Welsh councils, and Spanish, Balearic and other European municipalities.
problem: Levies are proliferating (Edinburgh in 2026, Glasgow from Jan 2027, Welsh councils from 2027, Balearics and Catalonia rising, Chicago at 19% hotel tax). Each council must register providers, collect returns, audit and chase non-payers, and most have neither software nor staff. Small B&Bs and self-caterers file badly and disputes pile up.
solution: A packaged portal for provider registration and returns, with support for per-night and percentage levies, exemptions, OTA-collected amounts and platform data feeds. It includes automated reminders, audit sampling, a provider help desk and a statutory report pack, configured per council within weeks.
why_now: New statutory levies start across the UK through 2026-27, and EU short-term rental rules require platforms to share host data with authorities from May 2026. That data can be matched against levy returns. Councils' levy revenue lets them fund administration.
revenue_model: GBP 20-60K per council per year, or a share of collected levy, plus per-return service fees for the help desk.
non_obvious_insight: Levies fail on administration rather than on rate-setting. Every council needs the same back office at the same moment, and levy revenue pays for it, so the customer has a budget line before it has a system.
first_30_days: Talk to 10 councils and the Welsh and Scottish local-government bodies. Offer a fixed-fee pilot of a provider portal and returns form for one small council. Build it from a form tool and a database first, then harden.

title: Trusted Firmware for Chinese-Made Robots
one_liner: A security-audited, network-isolated software and attestation layer that lets US labs, utilities and cities legally buy and run cheap Unitree-class robots.
customer: US universities and research labs, utilities, municipal fleets, critical-infrastructure operators, and integrators reselling Chinese quadrupeds and humanoids.
problem: Chinese makers hold 86% of humanoid shipments and their robots cost a fraction of US alternatives, but security teams block procurement over cloud telemetry, remote access and radio vulnerabilities disclosed in 2025. There is no neutral, certified 'clean' stack, and barriers are going up.
solution: A replacement software stack and wrapper: local-only operation, cloud services removed, wireless interfaces locked down, signed OTA updates under customer keys, an SBOM, and a continuous-audit attestation report that security auditors accept. Add an optional network-quarantine gateway appliance.
why_now: Tariffs, the FCC's DJI action and expected legislation are tightening. Unitree's IPO signals the supply will keep coming, so buyers with budgets are stuck between the price advantage and compliance.
revenue_model: $500-1,500 per robot a year for the license and updates, $10-30k per security assessment, and about $800 per gateway appliance.
non_obvious_insight: Each time the US restricts a Chinese hardware category, a trust layer becomes the only route for legal buyers. Everyone bets on which hardware wins, but the money sits in the compliance gap. Risk: an outright ban would kill the market, so design for a pivot to open-source or allied hardware.
first_30_days: Buy a Go2 and a G1, reproduce the publicly documented vulnerabilities, and publish a hardening guide. Offer free audits to 5 university robotics labs' IT security officers and convert 3 to paid assessments at $10-15k.

title: Agent-Buyable Assay Storefronts With QC-Gated Escrow
one_liner: Turn idle university cores and orphaned biotech labs into machine-buyable assay shops where payment releases automatically only if the raw instrument data passes pre-agreed control checks.
customer: Sellers are university core facilities, small CROs and shuttered-biotech labs with idle instruments. Buyers are protein-design, synbio and 'AI scientist' teams whose agents generate thousands of candidates. Revenue comes from a take rate on transactions.
problem: Design-build-test is now bounded by assays, not DNA (the Weizmann 2.5 billion antibody fragments cost only EUR 38,000 in DNA synthesis). Yet bench services are sold by 'request a quote' forms and PDF emails that agents cannot use, and buyers cannot judge whether a result is real. NIH turbulence (grant caps, K99 restrictions, staff protections stripped) and biotech layoffs (15,000+ cuts) leave cores and dead-company labs with idle capacity and no sales function. Agent commerce already shows the pattern: RentAHuman had about 590,000 sign-ups against about 11,300 bounties, so supply is abundant and trusted demand is scarce.
solution: Each standardized assay (BLI/SPR binding, thermal shift, expression titer, mycoplasma test, mass-spec ID, sequencing verification) becomes an MCP or ACP offer with price, turnaround, sample requirements, shipping label and acceptance criteria. Money sits in escrow and releases when deterministic rules on the raw output pass (positive/negative control window, Z' above a threshold, expected ladder). A failure triggers an automatic rerun or refund, so no one argues about disputes.
why_now: Machine-payment rails shipped in 2026 (Stripe/Tempo MPP on March 18, x402 to the Linux Foundation in April, ACP/AP2). Frontier labs are running hundreds of parallel bio-agents. NIH funding instability is pushing cores to seek outside revenue, and biotech distress in 2026 is creating idle labs.
revenue_model: 5-10% take rate on assay orders, float and expedite fees on escrow, listing setup fees for sellers ($500-2,000), and a managed-account tier for large protein-design teams.
non_obvious_insight: The unsolved dispute problem in agentic commerce becomes tractable for physical science because instruments emit machine-checkable controls. Acceptance tests on raw files stand in for human judgment, and academic core capacity is the cheapest, most trustworthy supply pool exactly when NIH money is shaky.
first_30_days: Sign 5 cores (mass spec, BLI, sequencing, flow) and list 10 SKUs with fixed prices. Run everything semi-manually behind a simple API and Stripe. Offer $2K free-assay bounties to 10 protein-design groups (BindCraft/RFdiffusion users) and have their scripts place orders. Publish pass rates and turnaround. Charge 8% from day one.

title: Independent Auditor for AI-Scribed Billing
one_liner: A continuous, coder-signed check on whether ambient AI scribe notes actually support the E/M levels being billed, before the payers or the government find out.
customer: Compliance officers, CFOs and revenue-integrity leaders at health systems and physician groups (20-500 providers), MSOs and PE-backed groups that rolled out ambient AI scribes. Secondary buyer: acquirers doing diligence on scribe-enabled practices.
problem: After ambient scribe rollouts, E/M distributions shift toward 99204-5 and 99214-5. Studies of six health systems show high-acuity visit share up roughly 12-20 points for new visits. Payers respond with AI downcoding and record requests, and the False Claims Act exposure is real if notes carry exam elements or time statements that did not happen. The scribe vendor cannot credibly audit itself, and annual compliance audits of 5-10 charts per provider cannot see systemic drift.
solution: Step 1 is a claims-only drift diagnostic (no EHR integration): compare each provider's E/M and modifier distribution before and after go-live with specialty benchmarks and peers, and rank the provider outliers. Step 2 is a targeted sample review by certified coders of the flagged encounters, checking that MDM or total-time really support the level. Copied-forward text, unsupported time attestations and orders without documented reasoning are the failure patterns. Step 3 is a continuing dashboard plus quarterly audit memos designed to be shown to a payer, auditor or the OIG. It includes a payer downcoding forecast.
why_now: Ambient scribes went mainstream across health systems in 2025-26. Research is documenting the coding-intensity increase and describing a payer-provider 'coding arms race', and payers are turning to their own AI for downcoding. The OIG's compliance program guidance expects organizations to audit new technology used in billing. Nobody independent has a standard offering yet.
revenue_model: $8-15 per audited encounter, or $15-30 per provider per month for the drift monitor plus sampled audits. Enterprise annual contracts of $50-200k. Diligence engagements at $10-25k each.
non_obvious_insight: The risk is not template bloat that scribes create in the HPI and exam. Under the 2021 E/M rules those elements do not count toward the level. The risk is that the scribe's fluent narration makes medical decision making and time statements sound stronger than what the physician did, and audits succeed or fail on MDM and time. Only coders who have survived payer audits know this. That is why a coder-signed audit is worth more than a model score, and why a compliance officer needs a third party, not the scribe vendor's coding module.
first_30_days: Find 3 mid-size groups, ideally with 30-100 providers, that adopted a scribe in the last 12 months, through LinkedIn outreach to compliance and revenue-integrity leads. Offer a free claims-only drift diagnostic, since 12 months of CPT data from their billing system is enough. Show them the outlier providers. Convert to a paid sample-audit engagement ($10-25k) and a monthly monitor. Recruit two certified auditors (CPC, CPMA) as contractors.

title: Thermal Safety Certification for Recovery Studios
one_liner: Staff certification, medication-aware intake screening and water-quality logging that insurers will soon require of sauna and cold-plunge operators.
customer: Contrast-therapy studios, gym recovery rooms, hotels and spas, paying monthly per location.
problem: Chain: studios are rolling out at speed (one brand added 25 locations in about 20 months and plans 100 more), so hundreds of new hires with no clinical training run 190F rooms and shared 40F tubs; customers increasingly take GLP-1s, blood-pressure meds or diuretics that raise fainting and dehydration risk; shared plunge water has no consistent standard and health departments are unsure how to classify it. One serious incident will trigger insurer exclusions and regulator attention.
solution: Three-part kit: a 90-minute 'Thermal Host' certification with annual refresh; tablet check-in screening (conditions and medications mapped to green/yellow/red session guidance plus waiver logging); and a water sensor pack (ORP, pH, chlorine, temperature) that auto-generates logs for inspectors and insurers.
why_now: The recovery boom (Nordic-style attendance up about 33 percent in 2025), mass GLP-1 use (about 1 in 8 adults), and no existing standard mean insurers and health departments are about to look for controls.
revenue_model: $99-199 per month per location, $39 per staff certification, sensor rental $49 per month per tub, plus insurer or broker referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Be the standard before the incident: insurers would rather subsidize a certification than write exclusions, and the screening data is a wedge to premium programs. GLP-1 plus heat is the specific collision no one is training for.
first_30_days: Draft the protocol with a sports-medicine physician and a pool-operations consultant, sell it to 5 independent studios in one metro at a discounted founding rate, and ask two studio-focused insurance brokers for a premium credit for certified locations.

title: Grandschools: Microschools Inside Senior Communities
one_liner: Turnkey K-8 microschools hosted in senior-living and 55+ communities, with residents as mentors and tuition funded by ESAs and scholarship credits.
customer: Senior-living operators and 55+ communities (pay a program fee for engagement and occupancy marketing); families paying tuition, ESA or scholarship dollars; retired professionals as mentors.
problem: More than 1,000 public schools closed in 2025-26, families are being displaced, and microschools struggle to find trusted adults (at Alpha School two-thirds of guides lack teaching credentials). Senior communities struggle with purpose-driven programming and occupancy. Each side has the resource the other lacks.
solution: A franchise-lite pilot model of 12-24 kids, 1 lead guide and 6-10 resident 'grand-mentors' (retired engineers, teachers, nurses) running project blocks, sharing dining, garden and library space. A standard playbook covers background checks, safeguarding, insurance, private-school registration and a mentor-hour ledger. Enrollment through ESA and SGO scholarships.
why_now: The demographic cliff in kids meets the aging peak. Scholarship credits and ESAs from 2027 make tuition viable for middle-income families, and the microschool guide shortage is acute.
revenue_model: $6-9k per child in tuition or ESA funds; operator program fee of $1-2k a month (or free space); licensing and playbook fees when replicating.
non_obvious_insight: The two halves of the demographic shift are each other's missing input: shrinking youth cohorts leave surplus buildings, growing elderly cohorts hold surplus expertise, and aging-services operators have engagement budgets that schools have never tapped.
first_30_days: Approach 10 independent-living communities in one metro that have on-site classrooms and sign one. Recruit 10 families from closed-school parent groups and a certified guide. Launch a 'Fridays' pilot before a full schedule. Confirm state private-school registration and insurance first.

title: Pre-Procedure GLP-1 Readiness for Endoscopy and Ortho
one_liner: A 7-day workflow plus day-of gastric ultrasound that stops GLP-1 patients from being cancelled or aspirating at surgery centers.
customer: GI endoscopy centers, orthopedic groups, ASCs and their anesthesia groups.
problem: ASA reversed course in Oct 2024 and now advises most patients to continue GLP-1s, shifting the risk to residual gastric contents on the day. Centers cancel or abort cases, and 38% of GLP-1 users vs 8% of non-users were malnourished before joint surgery, which raises complication risk. There is no standard workflow, so every center improvises.
solution: Automated intake (drug, dose, indication, GI symptoms), tailored liquid-diet and hold instructions aligned to multi-society guidance, a malnutrition screen with a protein prehab plan, and nurse-performed gastric POCUS with AI-assisted antral grading and documentation on the day. Priced per case.
why_now: With ~22% of households containing a user, this is routine, not exceptional. Gastric POCUS studies are appearing (2025-26) and centers are looking for a defensible protocol after the 2024 guideline change.
revenue_model: $60-150 per GLP-1 patient case, plus anesthesia-group license and ultrasound rental.
non_obvious_insight: Centers will not stop scheduling GLP-1 patients, so the value is avoided same-day cancellations (thousands of dollars each) and defensible documentation. The buyer is the center's operations and anesthesia leadership, not the drug companies.
first_30_days: Sell to one endoscopy center and one anesthesia group. Supply paper-plus-SMS intake, protocols, a rented handheld ultrasound and training. Track cancellation rate before and after and price at $75 per case.

title: Weather-Indexed Revenue Cover for Outdoor Micro-Businesses
one_liner: Per-day parametric policies that pay out within an hour when rain, heat or smoke hits a vendor's venue, priced from the vendor's own sales history.
customer: Farmers-market vendors, food trucks, festival vendors, ice cream and shaved-ice stands, seasonal farm stands and outdoor fitness operators.
problem: A rain day or heat wave can erase a day's sales and cannot be insured through conventional policies. Margins are thin, and small owners (about 64% of nonemployers in trouble) fall back on personal funds.
solution: Micro-policies bought per market day or season. A fixed payout triggers when measured rainfall, temperature or air quality at the venue exceeds a threshold during the market window. Premium and payout are calibrated to each vendor's baseline sales from POS or bank data, and payment goes out over instant rails. Distribution goes through market associations and POS apps.
why_now: Instant payout rails, POS and bank APIs for baseline sales, cheap gridded weather data, and reinsurer interest in parametric small-business products make this feasible for a small MGA team.
revenue_model: MGA margin on premiums of about $6-15 per vendor-day, plus program fees from market associations.
non_obvious_insight: Basis risk is manageable when triggers are set per venue and per day, and the product is cash within an hour of the rain rather than indemnity after paperwork. Vendors will buy small daily coverage bundled into their booth fee.
first_30_days: Partner with one market association (about 100 vendors) and an MGA or fronting carrier. Structure a season-long pilot under a master policy and price it from vendors' POS history. Track claims and basis risk.

title: Loss-Draft Concierge for Disaster Rebuilds
one_liner: A draw desk that gets the insurance money for a destroyed house out of the mortgage servicer's restricted account and into the rebuild, paid by the contractors who need cash to start.
customer: Mortgaged homeowners whose houses were destroyed or damaged by fire, flood or storm pay $1,500-3,000 flat or about 1% of proceeds. Rebuild contractors pay 1.5-2.5% of each accelerated draw.
problem: When a mortgaged house is destroyed, insurance checks are made out to both the owner and the servicer. The servicer parks the money in a loss-draft account and releases it in inspection-gated stages, each requiring a contract, contractor license proof, permits, lien waivers, W-9s and photos. Homeowners cannot assemble the packet. Contractors will not start without money. Families pay rent and a mortgage on a lot with nothing on it. Rebuild fraud thrives in the gap.
solution: A draw desk that takes the servicer's letter and builds the draw packet in the exact format the servicer wants. It verifies the contractor's license, collects conditional and unconditional lien waivers on the state statutory forms, books inspections, submits, and chases weekly. It escalates to servicer executive complaint lines and state regulators. It ties every disbursement to milestone photos and waivers so the homeowner is protected from paying for work not done. It never holds the funds, which avoids money-transmitter issues. Later add bridge financing against expected draws.
why_now: The January 2025 Los Angeles fires destroyed roughly 16,000 structures and rebuilds are now at peak permit and construction paperwork. Storm and flood rebuilds continue in Texas, North Carolina and Florida, and every season adds more. Additional-living-expense coverage has clocks that expire, which makes delay costly. AI document handling makes lien-waiver, permit and inspection-photo checks cheap for a small team.
revenue_model: Flat rebuild-admin package or about 1% of proceeds from homeowners. A per-draw acceleration fee of 1.5-2.5% from contractors. Later, a spread on bridge loans and referral revenue from lenders and builders.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not the insurer. The money already exists and is locked behind paperwork the homeowner cannot produce. Public adjusters take about 10% to fight the insurer but nobody specializes in this second fight. The hidden buyer is the contractor, whose cash flow decides whether the site ever starts.
first_30_days: Join fire-survivor community groups and rebuild nonprofits in one affected area. Offer a free draw-packet review to the first 10 households. Sign 3 rebuild contractors whose draws are stalled. Charge a flat fee only after the first draw is released. Document days-to-funds before and after as your proof, then take the case studies to the next disaster market.

title: Savings Groups as Verified Human Endpoints for Agents
one_liner: A group-guaranteed 'verify this physical fact' API, fulfilled by African savings groups and starting with solar and battery installations.
customer: Donor-funded energy-access results-based-financing programme administrators (who pay per verified installation), inverter and battery brands verifying warranties and distributor claims, and asset lenders and insurers. Agents that need physical facts are the long-term buyer.
problem: Agents can hire humans, but RentAHuman had about 590,000 sign-ups against about 11,300 active bounties and 5,500 completed jobs, plus scams and payment errors. Trusted agent demand is scarce because individual anonymous workers are a bad trust unit. Meanwhile Africa's distributed solar and battery boom (about 17 GW in 2026) is largely invisible: Ember's estimates are about 2x official statistics, and only 14 of 54 countries reported 2025 data. Lenders, insurers and utilities cannot verify what exists.
solution: A verify(system, location) API exposed as an MCP tool and payable by x402 or MPP. Fulfillment goes to savings groups (VSLAs and farmer groups), which already have joint-liability norms and a treasurer. Members capture device-attested photos, inverter-app screenshots, kWh readings and GPS. Random cross-checks by other members catch fraud, and a small bond from pooled savings backs each group. Payment goes to the group's mobile-money account, not to anonymous individuals.
why_now: The Hormuz energy shock and the solar and battery boom are pulling in subsidy programmes and lenders who need verification. Sandi AI shows 10,000+ farmer groups are already digitized in Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania. The public failure of agent-hiring marketplaces has created demand for a trust layer. Machine-payment protocols make per-task settlement cheap.
revenue_model: $4-8 per verification: about 65% to the group, 10% to the bond pool, 25% platform margin. Later, recurring data subscriptions on verified asset registries.
non_obvious_insight: Individuals are the wrong unit of trust for agent-issued work. A group with existing joint liability solves identity, fraud, payout and dispute in one move. Demand-first beats marketplace-first: RBF programmes already pay for verification today, so agents can be layered on afterwards.
first_30_days: Partner with an existing savings-group network (for example Sandi AI or a VSLA association) and onboard 20 groups in Uganda. Pitch one RBF administrator or battery distributor a 500-check pilot at $6 each. Run the verification workflow on WhatsApp and mobile money, with manual review of every submission.

title: Scan-Before-Buyout: Digital Memory and Game Assets
one_liner: Capture homes and streets in flood buyouts and burn zones in game-engine-grade 3D before demolition. The program pays for compliance and memorial; asset licensing to games and film is upside.
customer: County and state hazard-mitigation offices running buyouts, their historic-preservation consultants, and community foundations or long-term recovery groups funding memorials. Secondary buyers are game studios, VFX houses and XR training vendors.
problem: Buyouts demolish hundreds of 50-year-old homes. Federal funding triggers historic-property review, and the mitigation is often recorded documentation costing thousands per structure and producing a binder nobody opens. Families lose the physical record of their home and street, and the neighborhood dissolves undocumented. Only about 13% of affected Palisades owners have started rebuilding, so many lots sit for years. Game and film studios pay for authentic real-world environments that are hard to source.
solution: A crew of ex-game and VFX 3D artists uses Gaussian-splat or photogrammetry capture to scan exteriors, streetscapes and, with owner consent, interiors in an afternoon per home. Deliverables: (a) a compliance-grade documentation package, (b) a walkable keepsake file for each family, and (c) a de-identified 'American small-town' building kit licensed to studios, with revenue share to the community memorial fund.
why_now: Post-2024/25 flood buyouts are reaching demolition, and BRIC's $1B was reinstated in March 2026. Capture cost collapsed with splatting tools and phone-grade scanning. Game and VFX layoffs put skilled 3D artists on the market (Ubisoft headcount fell from 18,666 to 16,590 and EA's new owners plan AI-driven cost cuts), while studios need cheaper environment art.
revenue_model: Government or foundation contracts of $1,500-4,000 per structure or $40-150K per neighborhood, an optional $49 family keepsake often paid by a recovery fund, and five-figure per-studio licenses for the asset kit with revenue share to the county.
non_obvious_insight: The compliance mandate pays the bills, not the games market. Creative-industry tooling makes a documentation chore that nobody enjoys far cheaper, and turns it into a bereavement product and a licensable asset library. The county gets a better deliverable and a revenue share instead of a cost center.
first_30_days: Offer a free pilot street of 10 homes to a buyout manager in a post-flood region (western North Carolina or the Texas Hill Country). Collect owner releases. Deliver the splats plus a template mitigation stipulation a state preservation office can accept. Sell an anonymized kit on Fab, Sketchfab or the Unity store to test demand. Pitch consulting firms for subcontract work and a community foundation for the memorial grant.

title: Injection-Proof Video Calls for High-Stakes Approvals
one_liner: A WebRTC layer that accepts only video frames attested by the phone's secure hardware, killing virtual-camera and deepfake injection in notarizations and wire approvals.
customer: Remote online notarization platforms, title and escrow firms, banks' high-value approval calls, and later IDV vendors.
problem: Deepfake injection through virtual cameras, emulators and rooted devices defeats isolated liveness checks and video ID. Detection is a statistical arms race that decays with each new generator.
solution: An Android-first SDK and server verifier that checks device and app attestation (Key Attestation and Play Integrity, and App Attest on iOS for app integrity). Where the hardware supports it, it uses signed capture, then verifies that a session's frames come from an unmodified device and camera pipeline. It flags emulators and virtual cameras and runs beneath existing call providers.
why_now: Flagship phones now sign captured media (Pixel 10 Content Credentials, Samsung Galaxy S25 for AI edits). Injection attacks are now the standard route around IDV, and the CEN/TS 18099 injection-attack standard gives buyers a language for it.
revenue_model: $0.10-0.50 per attested session plus $2-10K per month platform fees.
non_obvious_insight: Detecting fakes is a losing game, while attesting the camera turns it into a cryptographic one. You do not need to sign the world's video, only the few sessions that move money or property.
first_30_days: Build the Android SDK and a demo, publish a red-team result against a virtual camera, approach 5 RON providers and title-tech firms, and run 3 paid pilots at about $2K per month.

title: Texted Pond-Algae and Forage-Poison Alerts for Ranchers
one_liner: Satellite imagery plus weather models watch every stock pond and frost-stressed sorghum field for the handful of killers that wipe out cattle in hours, then text the rancher and route the case to the vet.
customer: Ranchers and horse owners with ponds ($99-249 per year per operation). Bulk channels that pay: rural vet practices offering it as a client service, co-ops and feed dealers bundling it, livestock insurers and county extension programs (via grants) that want loss prevention.
problem: Every late summer and fall vets see clusters of cattle 'found dead' near stock ponds. Blue-green algae toxins kill within hours with no antidote, frost or drought-stunted sudangrass, johnsongrass and sorghum release prussic acid, and nitrates spike after a drought-breaking rain. Ranchers blame lightning, necropsy is rare, and the toxin is gone by the time a lab looks, so the losses are invisible in every statistic and nobody sells prevention. Existing satellite bloom tools target regulators and water bodies over about 1 square kilometer, not one-acre stock ponds.
solution: The rancher texts a location pin or uploads pasture boundaries. The service pulls free Sentinel-2 imagery (10 m resolution, roughly 5-day revisit), runs an open-source small-water-body cyanobacteria model (CyFi from the NASA/NOAA-backed research effort), layers local weather (frost forecast, rainfall after drought) and the forage type, and sends plain SMS: 'Pond in Pasture 4: bloom risk HIGH. Move cattle or run a trough. Your vet is Dr. X.' A one-tap 'I'm worried' reply routes a call to the vet's practice, which bills the visit. Vet-confirmed poisonings feed back to train the model, and later the product adds nitrate, ergot and heat-stress alerts.
why_now: Free 10 m satellite feeds, open ML models for small waterbodies and cheap cloud compute mean a two-person team can now do what used to need a research lab. Hotter summers and drought-then-flood cycles are raising bloom and forage-toxin risk, and with cows and bred heifers worth $3,000+ a five-head loss ($15K+) costs far more than the yearly subscription. Frost season (prussic acid) and late-season blooms are happening right now.
revenue_model: $149 per year per operation for unlimited ponds and pastures, a vet-channel wholesale price of about $2-3 per client per month with the practice keeping the resale margin plus referral visits, co-op bulk licenses, and loss-control contracts with mortality insurers who discount premiums for enrolled ranches.
non_obvious_insight: The rancher will never buy 'algae monitoring', but they will buy 'don't lose your cows'. Vets know that unexplained sudden-death clusters near ponds in August through October are dominated by cyanotoxins and forage toxicities, and that prevention (switch water, delay grazing) is trivial if the warning arrives before the herd does. Each vet-confirmed case is proprietary ground truth that public tools do not have, so accuracy compounds with every season.
first_30_days: Pilot with 20 ranches around 3 vet practices. Run CyFi plus Sentinel-2 on their ponds, and ground-truth flagged ponds with $30 cyanotoxin test strips and vet photos. Sell a $99 season pass through each vet's client newsletter and county extension agents, and time the launch for this fall's frost and late-bloom season. Record every alert, false positive and vet-confirmed case as the training and sales evidence for next summer.

title: Rights-Request Engine for Rejected Applicants
one_liner: A consumer tool that files legally formatted data-access and automated-decision requests to employers' hiring systems, turning silent rejections into scores, reasons and evidence.
customer: Job seekers, starting in the UK and EU under GDPR Art. 15/22, then Illinois and California. They pay $12 a month or $29 per request pack. Secondary buyers are plaintiff-side employment firms and researchers who license opt-in aggregate data.
problem: Applicants send dozens of applications, get almost no replies and never learn why (HN: 65 applications, 3 phone screens, 0 interviews). New laws give people rights to see and contest automated screening, but nobody uses them because finding the right contact and format is a hassle.
solution: A browser extension logs each application (company, ATS vendor, date). After 30 days of silence it files a data-access and automated-decision request, tracks the one-month deadline, escalates to the regulator, and parses the response into a structured 'why I was screened out' report. Opt-in aggregate stats show which employers and ATS vendors auto-reject which profiles.
why_now: California's automated-decision regulations start binding in Jan 2027 and Illinois' AI-in-employment notice law took effect Jan 2026. The Mobley v. Workday collective action is live and AI resume screening is ubiquitous. Job-search desperation is at a peak, and EU/UK rights already work today.
revenue_model: Consumer subscription or per-pack fees, plus opt-in anonymised data and insight licences to labor economists, unions and employment plaintiff firms. Employer-side compliance-readiness upsell later.
non_obvious_insight: Regulators created rights but no practical channel, and that friction is the enforcement gap. The service converts individual rights into aggregate leverage: an employer receiving 500 requests per role starts giving candidates real feedback, and the request-and-response dataset becomes the moat.
first_30_days: Build a GDPR-only MVP (templates, deadline tracker) for UK/EU applicants in two weeks, with a UK data-protection solicitor reviewing the templates. Seed it in UK and EU job-search communities and HN at £9 per pack. Measure response rates and refine.

title: Supply-House-Branded Back Office for Tiny Shops
one_liner: White-label quote, invoice, parts-pricing and trade-credit software delivered to solo-to-5-tech shops through their local independent supply house counter.
customer: Independent plumbing, HVAC, electrical and roofing supply houses and regional distributors squeezed by Home Depot (SRS, GMS, Mingledorff's) and Lowe's (FBM, Artisan). End users are their trade account holders.
problem: ServiceTitan fell about 26% after Q2 on slowing GTV, softer HVAC leads and a delay on exteriors, and expects only about 700 locations on its agentic tier. Most tiny shops have no operations layer and will not buy software cold, since CAC is brutal and churn high. Independent distributors are losing pro accounts to big-box integration and need a reason for contractors to stay.
solution: A private-label 'contractor OS' under the distributor's brand. Quotes are built from the distributor's live price book, invoices are text-to-pay, job notes and callbacks are tracked, truck stock reorders route to the counter, and net-30 parts credit is bundled. Counter staff onboard shops in person. It is free with a trade account, and the distributor pays per active shop.
why_now: Home Depot bought Mingledorff's in May 2026 on top of SRS and GMS, and Lowe's bought FBM for $8.8B. Independents' backs are against the wall. ServiceTitan's drop and deprioritization of exteriors leave small shops ignored. LLM-assisted development makes a lightweight tool cheap to build.
revenue_model: $30-60 per active shop per month paid by the distributor, or 0.25-0.5% of the shop's parts spend. Add payments interchange share and parts-financing spread.
non_obvious_insight: Vertical software wins on distribution. The supply house counter is the one place every tiny shop shows up every week, and distributors have both a strategic reason (defense against big-box) and a budget to pay for stickiness. Contractors will adopt anything that makes parts pricing and credit easier.
first_30_days: Sign two independent supply houses through buying-group contacts. Build an MVP on price-book CSV upload, SMS quotes and Stripe. Pilot with 20 shops per distributor and measure parts spend lift per shop.

title: Recall-Proofing Subscription for Small Pet Food Brands
one_liner: Outsourced food-safety plans, pooled H5N1/Salmonella/Listeria testing and label review for the hundreds of small raw, freeze-dried and topper brands that cannot afford a QA department.
customer: Small raw, freeze-dried, topper and mixer brands and their co-packers, including Shopify-native brands.
problem: FDA now requires makers of cat and dog food using uncooked or unpasteurized poultry, dairy or egg ingredients to reanalyze their food safety plans for H5N1 under the animal-food preventive controls rule, after cats died from contaminated raw food. A recall can kill a small brand, and the fast-growing topper and mixer category (purchases +214% since 2018 per the briefing) creates label and 'complete and balanced' compliance ambiguity.
solution: A monthly subscription with PCQI-qualified plan writing and upkeep, supplier verification, a pooled testing program at negotiated lab prices with a certificate-of-analysis dashboard, mock-recall drills and label review against current AAFCO and state rules. Bundle with a recall-insurance partner for lower premiums.
why_now: FDA's H5N1 reanalysis requirement (announced January 2025) turned a news event into a permanent compliance line item. DTC consolidation (Farmer's Dog's first acquisition) raises supplier-diligence standards for small brands seeking exits.
revenue_model: $500-2,000 per month subscription, 20-30% margin on pooled testing pass-through, and insurance referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders treat H5N1 as an outbreak headline. For small brands it is a permanent, recurring cost, and testing volume can be pooled across many brands to get lab prices and QA depth no single brand can afford, the same economics that supports outsourced food-safety consultants in human food.
first_30_days: List 300 raw and freeze-dried brands from FDA registration and social listings. Send a free H5N1 gap audit against FDA's reanalysis requirement. Contract a PCQI consultant and one accredited lab. Convert 5-10 brands to paid subscriptions.

title: Privacy-Compliant Monetization for Faith Apps
one_liner: An audit-plus-replacement stack for small prayer, Quran, Bible, Torah and temple apps whose ad SDKs quietly turn every user into a sale of religious-belief data.
customer: Independent and mid-size publishers of ad-funded faith apps (prayer times, Quran, Bible/devotional, Hindu calendar, Zmanim, halal finders, congregation apps) and church-management/giving software vendors serving thousands of congregations.
problem: Religious beliefs are special-category data under GDPR Art. 9 and 'sensitive data' requiring opt-in consent under nearly every US state privacy law. Maryland's law goes further, banning the sale of sensitive data and limiting collection to what is strictly necessary (in force since Oct 2025, verify enforcement dates). Regulators have treated mere use of a niche app as revealing sensitive traits (Norway's Grindr fine, upheld on appeal, verify). Reporting in 2020 showed a Muslim prayer app's location data reaching a broker and then US military contractors. Yet most small faith apps run stock ad SDKs with device IDs and location, have no consent flow and no counsel. The briefing notes non-Christian faith apps are far less served than Hallow-style Christian ones, and the IAPP says state privacy momentum is at an all-time high.
solution: (1) A public audit tool that scans app binaries and web properties for SDK data flows and issues a scorecard plus a legal-risk memo by state and EU. (2) A drop-in compliance SDK: a consent manager that treats every user as sensitive by default, server-side region logic, data maps and DPIA templates in Arabic, Urdu, Bahasa, Hebrew, Spanish and Portuguese. (3) A contextual, ID-free sponsorship marketplace where halal, kosher, umrah, church-goods and faith-nonprofit sponsors book placements by content context (for example an iftar-times page). (4) A subpoena and data-request playbook with minimal retention by design, so the app has little to hand over.
why_now: State privacy laws with sensitive-data opt-in are now the norm and Maryland's strict rules are enforceable in 2026 (verify dates). GDPR fines total EUR 7.16B with 229 new cases in 2026 (per briefing). Faith apps are booming (Hallow reached #1 in the US App Store) while faith data is politically charged around surveillance and immigration enforcement.
revenue_model: $149-499/month per app for SDK plus audit. 25-30% revenue share on contextual sponsorship. One-time $1.5-3k audit and fix sprint. Enterprise contracts with church-tech vendors.
non_obvious_insight: For a faith app the category itself reveals the belief (the Grindr logic), so 'we do not collect religion' is not a defense. The violation is the ad model, so the fix is a different revenue stream, not a policy PDF. Contextual sponsorship from faith-community advertisers can pay better than junk programmatic. Public scorecards create the sales funnel, because in tight communities reputation and fear move fast.
first_30_days: Audit the top 100 Muslim prayer/Quran apps and 50 Christian, Jewish and Hindu apps with open-source traffic analysis (mitmproxy, Exodus-style trackers). Publish a 'Privacy Scorecard for Faith Apps' and email each publisher. Sell paid fix sprints to 5 pilot apps at about $2k and recruit 5 community sponsors for contextual placements. Team is one privacy lawyer plus one Android engineer.

title: Audit-Proof Family Night in a Box
one_liner: Fixed-price, compliance-packaged family engagement events for Title I schools, paid from the federally required parent-engagement set-aside, with the monitoring binder as the real product.
customer: District Title I coordinators and Title I principals. The money comes from the ESSA parent and family engagement reserve, which is 1 percent of Title I for districts above the size threshold, and most of it must go to schools.
problem: That money is earmarked but scary to spend. Principals fear audit findings over food, childcare, transport, interpreters and incentives, because each has 'necessary and reasonable' tests and must tie back to the district's engagement policy and the school-parent compact. Events get thin turnout of 20 to 30 percent of families. Principals end up buying pizza with sketchy funds, or the money sits unspent until spring.
solution: A fully produced event in a box. It is built around students performing or presenting, and includes a dinner from a local caterer, on-site childcare, ride vouchers, live interpreters and a personal invitation call script. Every event ships with a pre-vetted allowable-cost memo, an agenda tied to the compact and policy, QR sign-in, a parent needs survey, an evaluation report and a monitoring-ready binder generated automatically. Packages are $4.5k to $9k per event, with annual bundles for a district.
why_now: After the July 2025 federal funding freeze scare and post-ESSER budget cuts, coordinators are under pressure to spend every Title I dollar on time and defensibly. Chronic absenteeism has stuck near one in four students, and family engagement is the best-evidenced lever schools have left. States are also stepping up monitoring of federal-funds documentation.
revenue_model: Per-event fixed fee ($4.5k to $9k), annual multi-event contracts ($25k to $60k per school), and a district-wide compliance template license.
non_obvious_insight: Turnout comes from four things nobody bundles: kids on stage, food, childcare in the building, and a personal call from a known adult. The real blocker is not attendance. It is the principal's fear of an audit finding, so the binder is what they are buying and the event is only the delivery vehicle. Vendors that sell 'parent engagement software' miss this because the software cannot make an allowable-cost decision.
first_30_days: Read one state's Title I monitoring protocol and write a two-page allowable-cost memo. Get two Title I coordinators to comment on it and agree to a template. Pitch 5 principals you know, and run 3 pilot events at cost with a local caterer and a bilingual emcee. Capture turnout data versus the school's usual events. Turn the paperwork into a reusable binder generator.

title: Signed Live Recordings from Every Small Venue
one_liner: A cheap box that records a small venue's mixing-desk multitrack, signs it with time and place, and delivers the artist a 'recorded live tonight' release within hours.
customer: Touring indie artists (per-show packages) and small venues of 25-500 capacity (hosts and revenue partners), later promoters and ticketing.
problem: The one thing AI cannot fabricate is a specific night in a specific room. Yet tens of thousands of small shows happen nightly with no recording, while generative music floods the shelf. Bandcamp's AI ban made it a natural home for human-made music, and artists have few new products to sell there.
solution: Software on a mini-PC or a $300-500 box connects to common digital consoles (Behringer X32/Midas-class, Allen & Heath) over USB or network to capture multitrack audio. It timestamps with network time and location, signs a C2PA audio manifest, auto-mixes with ML, and delivers a release and shareable page within hours. Venues get a share of sales, and a public ledger builds over time.
why_now: C2PA supports audio, generative music has made 'real and live' a scarcity signal, cheap mini-PCs and ML auto-mixing exist, and Bandcamp is positioned as a human-only marketplace.
revenue_model: $99-199 per show for the artist, or $79/month per venue plus 20% of release sales, with hardware leased at about $399.
non_obvious_insight: Provenance of place and time is unforgeable in a way that process proof is not. A live album also turns authenticity into a revenue-producing product instead of a cost.
first_30_days: Wire up 5 friendly venues in one city with X32 consoles. Hand-mix the first shows. Sell 'live release in 24 hours' to 20 touring bands at $99 through booking agents, and track Bandcamp sales.

title: Real Gross Margin Diligence for AI Startups
one_liner: Quality-of-earnings for agent companies: restate COGS at unsubsidized token prices, retry waste and expiring credits so investors see true unit economics.
customer: Growth-equity, PE and VC diligence teams and corporate M&A groups acquiring AI-native companies ($20M-$500M deals), and startups preparing a raise.
problem: Reported AI gross margins are flattered by free cloud and model credits, introductory rates and uncosted retries. Practitioners say diligence restates credits at renewal prices, and AI-native margins run around 50-60% versus 75-85% for classic SaaS. Agentic tasks use 5-30x more tokens, so cohort economics move fast. M&A is heating up (Okta bought Permiso for about $200M in July 2026, and Palo Alto bought Portkey and Koi). Traditional QoE firms lack telemetry fluency.
solution: Read-only connectors to billing exports, gateways, cloud invoices and product analytics. Produce cohort-level unsubsidized COGS per seat or outcome, sensitivity to price cuts and model swaps, tokens per customer growth, cost of failed runs and retries, and scaling curves. Five-day turnaround report, plus quarterly monitoring for fund portfolios.
why_now: An AI M&A wave and investors pricing trajectory over current margin. Credit-inflated margins matter more as promotional pricing expires, and 73% of enterprises overran AI budgets.
revenue_model: $15-$40k per diligence engagement and $3-$8k/month portfolio monitoring subscriptions for funds.
non_obvious_insight: The margin story is hidden in gateway and billing logs, not the general ledger. Buyers pay a premium to avoid overpaying for subsidized revenue, and every engagement builds a private benchmark of credit-adjusted margins.
first_30_days: Write the data-request list and report template. Pitch 20 growth-stage funds and deal associates, deliver 2 discounted diligence reports, and publish an anonymized credit-adjusted gross margin benchmark to generate inbound.

title: Tenant Childcare Consortium Powered by 45F Credits
one_liner: Turn a vacant floor in a multi-tenant office or medical office building into a shared licensed childcare center whose seats are bought by 10-40 small tenant employers, each claiming the expanded 45F credit through a landlord-led consortium.
customer: Landlords of class-B office and medical office buildings (setup and management fee), small employers in those buildings (compliance fee and seat purchases), and a specialist childcare operator.
problem: Office vacancy is 17.8% nationally and lenders face $39B of office debt maturing in 12 months, so landlords need sticky tenants. Small employers cannot justify their own center. From 2026 the 45F credit is 40% (50% for small businesses) of qualified childcare spending, capped at $500K ($600K), and the law now lets an intermediary contract with childcare facilities for several employers. Almost no one has built the intermediary. Hospitals, clinics and professional-services firms in medical office buildings have severe shift-worker childcare gaps.
solution: The landlord donates or discounts a vacant suite (ideally lower floors) and a TI allowance. A licensed operator runs the center. The platform acts as the intermediary entity: it signs seat contracts with 10-40 tenants, documents each employer's qualified expenditure for the credit (Form 8882), pools and re-allocates unused seats among tenants, and helps employees route the DCFSA. A third-party operator whose principal business is childcare also sidesteps the 30%-employee-enrollment test that trips up in-house employer centers (to be confirmed with tax counsel).
why_now: The OBBBA expansion took effect for tax years beginning after Dec 31, 2025, so employers are setting 2026 and 2027 budgets now, and the year-end rush to lock 2026 credits is a natural sales moment. Landlords are under maturity-wall pressure and compete on amenities.
revenue_model: Landlord setup fee plus an NOI share of the operating margin (about 10%), a per-employer compliance fee (3-5% of credit value), and operator management fees.
non_obvious_insight: The credit turns a landlord amenity into a purchasing cooperative: alone a 40-person tenant cannot justify a center, but 20 together can, and the credit is richest for exactly the small businesses that fill class-B buildings. A child's seat is also far stickier than free rent as a lease-renewal driver, because losing the lease means losing the seat.
first_30_days: Approach five owners of medical office buildings and suburban office parks with 20%+ vacancy in a high-cost childcare metro. Survey tenants with a two-question form to size seat demand. Line up an operator and a tax counsel opinion memo. Aim to sign 8-10 employer seat contracts before December 2026 so they capture credits for this tax year.

title: Crash-Test Ratings for Collusive Pricing Agents
one_liner: A simulation lab and clean-room negotiation venue that certifies your pricing or negotiating agent does not tacitly collude with counterpart agents, like Euro NCAP for antitrust.
customer: General counsel, antitrust counsel and pricing or procurement heads at companies deploying pricing or negotiation agents: property managers and landlords, hotels, insurers, freight brokers, ad-buying agencies and retailers. Pricing-software vendors who are being sued are the first buyers.
problem: Two LLM agents that repeatedly interact can converge on supracompetitive prices with no human ever agreeing to anything. The law is moving fast: California's AB 325 took effect January 1, 2026, the DOJ RealPage settlement landed in late 2025, and DOJ officials said in May 2026 that 'software cannot launder collusion'. Deployers have no way to show their agent is clean.
solution: A harness that plays your agent against a zoo of counterpart agents (clones of itself, competitor-like agents, vendor agents) across thousands of repeated-game scenarios. It measures price convergence, punishment and signaling patterns, and information leakage, and issues a rated report plus CI regression tests. A hosted clean-room negotiation venue firewalls competitors' inputs and keeps regulator-readable logs. Partner economists and an antitrust firm sign the report.
why_now: AB 325 and its lowered pleading standard, active DOJ and state enforcement, private class actions over pricing algorithms, and agent-to-agent negotiation going live with the 2026 commerce protocols. Academic work has shown LLM pricing agents can settle on collusive outcomes without instruction.
revenue_model: $25-150k per audit, $2-5k per month for CI-integrated monitoring, and expert-witness and defense-support add-ons revenue-shared with partner economists.
non_obvious_insight: The exculpatory evidence is counterfactual behavior: what your agent would do if a rival raised its price. Only the deployer can generate that evidence, and it is cheap to produce in simulation, so antitrust compliance can be turned into unit tests. Because plausible-agreement pleading is now enough to survive dismissal, having a dated, third-party test record is worth far more than its price.
first_30_days: Team up an industrial-organization economist and an antitrust lawyer. Publish an open 'collusion eval' benchmark of LLM repeated pricing games to build credibility. Pitch 10 rental-pricing, hospitality and freight-pricing software vendors a $25k fixed-fee 'pre-litigation' audit and close the first two within about 60 days.

title: Diabetes Desk: Remote Glucose-Curve Review for Clinics
one_liner: CGMs and once-daily insulins made diabetic pets manageable at home, but nobody owns the workflow; sell clinics an outsourced desk that reads curves and proposes titrations for the DVM to approve.
customer: General-practice clinics with a dozen or more insulin-dependent dogs and cats. Secondary: pet insurers with diabetic cohorts.
problem: AAHA's 2026 guidelines split canine and feline diabetes for the first time and emphasize CGMs and once-daily insulins (degludec, glargine U-300). Owner burden is high and remote-monitoring services are thin. Clinics get a stream of curves they have neither the time nor a billing model to review, so pets stay poorly regulated. Tight control gives diabetic cats a real chance of remission, and avoids expensive ketoacidosis emergencies.
solution: Owners link a CGM to a clinic-branded portal. A desk of RVTs plus a consulting internist reviews curves weekly, flags hypoglycemia risk, and drafts dose-change suggestions for the clinic's own vet to approve within their VCPR. Includes SMS coaching on feeding and injection technique and refill/supply coordination. The clinic bills the owner a monthly program fee and pays us a wholesale share.
why_now: 2026 AAHA guidelines make CGM standard-of-care thinking. Long-acting insulins reduce injection burden. Ambient AI makes the record-keeping cheap, and remote-care rules are loosening piecemeal.
revenue_model: Clinic charges owners $59-99 per month; we take about $30-45 per patient per month. Later: outcome-based contracts with insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The clinical tech (CGMs, insulins, guidelines) arrived before the operating model. Human remote-monitoring took years to get billing codes; in vet medicine the owner pays directly and the value (fewer ER visits) is visible immediately, so a desk business can start without any payer.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 clinics and about 20 diabetic patients. Run a manual desk with one contract RVT and a part-time internist consult. Use CGM sharing links or screenshots to start. Track time-in-range and ER visits, and price the pilot at $79 per month.
